                                              PROJECT NO. 58000

 RULEMAKING TO UPDATE                                        §    PUBLIC UTILITY COMMISSION
 WHOLESALE AND IOU RETAIL                                    §
 TRANSMISSION COST RECOVERY IN                               §                   OF TEXAS
 THE ERCOT REGION                                            §


        CRUSOE ENERGY SYSTEMS LLC COMMENTS ON PROPOSAL FOR
      PUBLICATION OF AMENDMENTS TO §25.192 and §25.193 and NEW §25.252

         Crusoe Energy Systems LLC (“Crusoe”) files these comments on the Public Utility
Commission of Texas (“Commission”) Proposal for Publication of the proposed amendments to
16 Texas Administrative Code (“TAC”) §25.192 relating to Transmission Rates for Export from
ERCOT and §25.193 relating to Distribution Service Provider Transmission Cost Recovery
Factors (“TCRF”), and new §25.252 relating to Large Load Customer Tariffs (“Proposal”). Crusoe
is a vertically integrated infrastructure company that takes an “energy-first” approach to building
solutions. Crusoe is a significant contributor to projects in Texas, representing billions of dollars
in investment and creating thousands of local jobs in the coming years.

                                              I.       INTRODUCTION
         Crusoe supports the Commission’s fundamental objective of protecting other customers
from grid infrastructure costs caused by large-load development. Large loads, like all loads, should
pay for the costs they cause. Likewise, large loads, like all other loads, should not pay for costs
they do not cause. Indeed, while incorporating large loads into the existing grid poses novel
challenges that call for some novel approaches, such as the ERCOT Batch Zero process and the
reexamination of reliance on 4CP, bedrock principles such as fairness of apportionment, avoidance
of undue discrimination, understandability, stability, and predictability remain sufficiently durable
to continue to provide guardrails to the rates designed to apply to large loads.1
         Mindful of these guardrails, Crusoe provides these comments, not in opposition to the
Commission’s Proposal, but rather to suggest some aspects of the Proposal that Crusoe submits
could be calibrated to ensure that large loads pay for the costs they cause but not be subject to
punitive, duplicative, or discriminatory charges that are not demonstrated to be caused by system
impacts. Crusoe supports, for example, the Commission proposal to modernize transmission cost

         1

 allocation, including a 12CP or similar methodology that continues to provide stimulus for demand
response, but results in less skewing of the allocation of transmission costs. Crusoe likewise
supports a reasonable minimum transmission charge for large load customers as layered protection
for other customers, provided that the charge is calibrated to the risks or costs imposed by the large
load that are not otherwise financed or secured. Crusoe therefore recommends that the Commission
modify provisions that are not calibrated to risk, including the proposed 20-year minimum billing
demand, automatic pre-energization billing, treatment based on full reserved capacity regardless
of phased development or ramp schedules, and separate rate treatment based solely on large
computational load status.

                                  II.     GENERAL COMMENTS
    A. Any Minimum Payment Requirement Should Be Calibrated to the Outstanding Risks
         or Costs.

    Once a customer has posted security, executed an interconnection agreement, paid required
direct costs, and provided the customer remains in compliance with its obligations, the customer
should not be presumed to be imposing unjustified costs on the system. Any additional measures
should be imposed only if and when proven necessary to protect ratepayers, so the additional
measures do not constitute a discriminatory or unfair penalty or a taking of private property.

    Crusoe does not oppose a minimum payment, provided that the minimum payment is a
calibrated backstop. But the proposed use of full contracted demand as the automatic minimum
billing demand is overinclusive. Contracted demand measures reservation rights, not unrecovered
cost or actual cost responsibility. A minimum payment should instead net unrecovered risk after
CIAC, unrefunded security, interconnection fees, ordinary transmission charges, energization
status, and phased development are taken into account. As noted in the Commission’s assessment
of the public benefits of the proposed rules, one of the goals of this proceeding is to “ensur[e] that
transmission cost recovery appropriately charges the system costs that are caused by each customer
class.”2 Crusoe supports this goal and a minimum payment that is consistent with it. But reliance
on a proxy for the unpaid and unsecured costs that ignores both the presence and amount of
carefully crafted existing financial protections is, at best, a broad swag based on systemwide

         2
             Proposal at 4.

HB: 4899-5946-6429.5
 averages that fails to ascertain or allocate the particular costs and risks imposed by a particular
customer.

    B. Four Proposed Modifications to Calibrate a Minimum Payment Requirement.

    Crusoe recommends changing the proposed rule in three ways. First, Crusoe recommends
separating “minimum payment” from “minimum billing demand.”                The Proposal currently
converts the minimum payment into a deemed billing demand equal to the greater of contracted
peak demand, highest NCP, or 12CP. This proposal disassociates the minimum payment from
cost or risk caused.        Instead, Crusoe recommends defining the obligation as a minimum
transmission payment calculated to recover a calculated residual risk or cost, after accounting for
CIAC, financial security, interconnection fees, and ordinary transmission charges. A uniform
minimum billing demand is a blunt proxy rather than a true cost-causation mechanism.

    Second, Crusoe recommends that, if contracted demand is used as one input in calculating a
minimum payment, the Commission modify the role of contracted demand in determining the
minimum payment and instead use it only as either a cap or a starting point, and not as an automatic
billing floor. Contracted peak demand may be relevant because it reflects reserved capacity. To
provide a reasonable measure of cost or risk, however, the minimum payment should be adjusted
for energization status, phased ramp schedules, actual 12CP/NCP usage, and financial protections
already posted.        Under this approach, the actual payment would be calculated based on a
percentage of contracted demand and would decline over time or shift toward actual 12CP demand.

    Third, the use of an estimate of costs and risks based on a systemwide average should be used
as a proxy for the costs and risks imposed by a load only as a last resort and only if supported by
findings that calculating the actual cost and risk imposed by a particular load are incalculable, or
at least impracticable to calculate. Use of a proxy is administratively easier, but ensures both over
and under recoveries.

    Fourth, as noted above, and to ensure that the required relationship between cost causation or
risk avoidance is preserved, Crusoe recommends that the Commission require any minimum
payment calculation include offsets for amounts already paid or secured through CIAC, forfeited
security, interconnection fees, and amounts recovered through rates. In this way, the Commission

                                            Page 3 of 27
HB: 4899-5946-6429.5
 can achieve its customer protection objective without imposing duplicative or punitive payment
obligations on large load customers.

    C. Pre-Energization Charges, If Any, Should Be Calibrated to Cost or Risk.

    Crusoe has similar concerns regarding the commencement of minimum billing before
energization. To be clear, Crusoe supports the Commission’s goal of protecting other customers
from the risk that transmission capacity is reserved or facilities are constructed for a large load that
does not timely energize. However, financial security should be calibrated to the utility’s
unrecovered exposure during the pre-energization period without imposing ongoing deemed-
demand charges that commence before service even begins.

    Before energization, the large load customer’s primary risk to other customers is not unpaid
usage; it is nonperformance, abandonment, or failure to proceed after the utility has incurred costs
or reserved capacity. Properly sized financial security is a more direct and calibrated tool for that
risk than deemed billing at contracted demand, and the proposed rules already require substantial
protections for that risk, including CIAC, interconnection fees, financial security, and long-term
contractual commitments. Where those protections are properly sized and enforceable, they should
protect the utility and other customers without requiring the customer to begin making ongoing
deemed-demand payments before it is able to take service.                        At most, therefore, any pre-
energization minimum payment should be limited to a residual backstop for demonstrated,
unsecured risk, limited to the net unrecovered exposure remaining after CIAC, interconnection
fees, financial security, and other contractual remedies are taken into account, and should
commence only when the capacity is actually usable by the customer and any failure to energize
is within the customer’s control.3

    Finally, billing should not automatically begin merely because capacity is theoretically
available if the customer has not energized, facilities are only partially available, or readiness is
affected by utility construction timing or phased development. A more calibrated approach would



         3
           “Available” capacity may not always mean usable, deliverable, fully tested, or available for the full
contracted amount. A pre-energization billing trigger could invite disputes about whether service is actually
available and at what level.


                                                   Page 4 of 27
HB: 4899-5946-6429.5
 commence billing after energization, customer acceptance of available facilities, an agreed
readiness milestone, or at least availability of capacity actually capable of serving the customer.

    D. An Alternative “More Calibrated” Minimum Demand Charge.

    As discussed, it is Crusoe’s view that the financial security for system upgrades required
through the Commission’s proposed rule in Project 58481 is designed to protect residential and all
other customers from bearing the transmission system upgrade costs caused by large loads and
that, if an additional charge is required, it need not be demand based. If the Commission
nonetheless determines that a numerical minimum demand payment floor is necessary, accurately
or adequately reflects cost causation, and is not punitive, a more calibrated approach would be to
establish a lower, time-limited minimum charge. For example, a charge based on approximately
50% of reserved demand for approximately five years, subject to adjustment for phased
energization, actual usage, CIAC, posted financial security, interconnection fees, and amounts
otherwise recovered through rates, would better reflect the fact that stranded-cost risk is highest
during the early project period and declines as the customer energizes, costs are recovered, and
actual usage becomes a more reliable measure of cost responsibility.4 Any phase-down could be
tied to elapsed time, unrecovered transmission investment, energization milestones, actual load
ramp, or a combination of those factors.

    Even at a rate more closely calibrated to the residual risk, imposition of even a reduced charge
in advance of energization raises the same issues discussed above related to charging for deemed
service before service is taken. A better solution may be to allow the charge to start only when
capacity is actually usable and the delay is within the customer’s control, or if it applies pre-
energization, only as a residual backstop after financial security is credited in accordance with
Commission rules. Crusoe would urge the Commission to apply a net-risk approach, regardless
of the level at which the minimum payment is set, as a 50% rate may be less punitive than 100%,
but it can still be duplicative and unwarranted if CIAC and posted security already cover the
TDU/TSP’s exposure. The 50% / 5-year concept is a more calibrated alternative to the proposed
100% / 20-year demand ratchet. However, it is not a substitute for the Commission also addressing

          4
            If a project has phased reserved capacity, the 50% should apply to the then-available/usable phase and
not to the full ultimate project demand.


                                                   Page 5 of 27
HB: 4899-5946-6429.5
 commencement, offsets, financial security, and phased development. Regardless of the form or
timing of the minimum charge, it should operate only as a residual backstop for demonstrated,
unsecured risk of increased costs of the transmission system cost of service.

    Crusoe submits that these recommendations ensure other customers are protected from the
costs and risks imposed by large loads, through a backstop minimum payment calibrated to
residual risk and cost, rather than a punitive demand ratchet. Crusoe has proposed revisions to §
25.193(d)(2) and § 25.252(e)(2) to reflect these recommendations.

                       III.   RESPONSES TO COMMISSION’S QUESTIONS
    1. Should the values associated with the large load minimum billing demand provisions
       be different for large load customers with different contracted peak demands or
       different non-coincident (NCP) demands?

    While Crusoe contends that the proposed large load minimum billing demand is not adequately
calibrated to the costs and risks a particular large load causes, Crusoe supports differentiated
minimum billing that reflects different costs or risks imposed. If the Commission chooses to
impose minimum billing demand charges, different minimum billing demand values may be
appropriate if differences in contracted peak demand or NCP demand correspond to different
transmission cost responsibility, reserved capacity, or stranded-cost risk. But the rule should not
impose harsher treatment on larger loads simply because they are larger. A rule that charges larger
loads more simply for being large, without reference to the transmission investment they actually
trigger, does not track cost causation and could be read as arbitrary under PURA §36.003.
    Any minimum billing demand should be calibrated to cost causation, actual or reserved
transmission impacts, phased development, and should take into account the extent to which other
protections—such as financial security, CIAC, interconnection agreements, or other contractual
commitments—already protect other customers from unrecovered costs. As discussed in Crusoe’s
general comments, above, the structure and amount of a minimum bill should reflect cost and risk
only, and runs the risk of being punitive if it is unrelated to costs or risks, or is duplicative of other
payments or security. A rigid billing floor based only on the size of the load risks disconnection
from actual cost or residual risk.
    A better alternative for differentiating minimum bills would be to rely on the known-cost
waterfall methodology ERCOT already employs in determining Batch Zero system-upgrade
security (RPG pro-rata cost per MW; LLIS but-for upgrade cost; $0 where a TSP/DSP attests no
upgrades are required; a $50,000/MW backstop only where costs are genuinely unknown) rather
than a size-based differentiation.


                                              Page 6 of 27
HB: 4899-5946-6429.5
     2. Should the large load minimum billing demand be:

              a. fixed for 20 years as proposed;

              b. reduced in phases over a period of 20 years; or

              c. extended to a longer time period?
         Crusoe recommends that the Commission modify the proposed minimum billing
requirement so that it operates as a calibrated, time-limited backstop rather than a fixed 20-year
obligation at the same level. Crusoe supports the Commission’s objective of protecting other
customers from unrecovered transmission costs or reserved-capacity risk, but the amount and
duration of any minimum billing requirement should be tied to the customer’s actual project status,
approved ramp schedule, and declining residual risk. A rigid 20-year minimum billing obligation
based on full contracted peak demand, maximum NCP demand, or 12CP demand is likely broader
than necessary to protect other customers and may operate as a punitive or duplicative charge
rather than a calibrated cost-recovery mechanism.
         A better approach would allow minimum billing to phase in with the customer’s approved
energization and ramp schedule, and then phase out as the customer transitions to ordinary 12CP
treatment. For phased projects, the minimum billing amount should be based on the then-available
and usable phase of service, not the customer’s full ultimate contracted demand before that
capacity is energized or capable of being used.
         Crusoe supports consideration of a 50%/five-year approach as a more calibrated alternative
to the proposed 100%/20-year obligation, provided the 50% level applies only to the relevant
energized, available, or usable phase and is offset by CIAC, interconnection fees, posted or
forfeited security, ordinary transmission payments, and other protections that reduce residual risk.
After the initial risk period, the customer should transition toward ordinary 12CP treatment,
because actual coincident peak usage becomes the more appropriate measure of transmission cost
responsibility as the project energizes, ramps, and becomes integrated into the ERCOT system.


    3. Should the large load minimum billing demand be based on some measure of demand

         lower than contracted peak demand and NCP demand? For example, should the large

         load minimum billing demand:


                                           Page 7 of 27
HB: 4899-5946-6429.5
               a. reflect a “ratcheted” demand, wherein the large load minimum billing demand

                   is some percentage of the customer’s contracted peak demand or maximum

                   NCP demand in the previous year? If so, should the ratchet percentage decline

                   in phases over the years, and how?

              b. be based on a “weighted average” minimum billing demand, wherein the large
                   load minimum billing demand is some weighted average of the large load
                   customer’s contracted peak demand or highest NCP demand over the previous
                   year and the large load customer’s 12CP demand? If so, should the percentage
                   weighting towards contracted peak demand or NCP demand decline in phases
                   over the years, and how?
         Crusoe recommends that the Commission not treat contracted peak demand or prior-year
NCP demand as an irrebuttable measure of large-load cost responsibility. Contracted demand and
NCP demand may be relevant inputs because they can indicate reserved capacity or site-level
demand, but demand is not the same thing as cost causation. Standing alone, these demand
measures do not establish the net unrecovered transmission costs or stranded-capacity risks caused
by a particular customer. The purpose of any minimum billing requirement should be to hold other
customers harmless from costs caused by the large load, not to assign to large loads costs they did
not cause.
    That distinction is important. To the extent residential customers are currently bearing a
disproportionate share of transmission costs, that is a problem that predates the arrival of large
loads in large numbers and should be addressed through generally applicable cost-allocation
reform. It is no more consistent with bedrock cost-causation principles to shift costs to large loads
that they did not cause than it is to misallocate transmission costs to residential customers. Cost
causation protects all customer classes; it is not satisfied by moving costs from one class to another
unless the shifted costs are shown to be caused by that class.
    For that reason, Crusoe’s primary recommendation is not to replace the Proposal’s 100%/20-
year demand ratchet with a different flat demand ratchet. Crusoe recommends that the Commission
separate minimum billing from minimum billing demand and require any minimum payment to be
calibrated to demonstrated, residual, unsecured risk after accounting for CIAC, interconnection
fees, posted or forfeited financial security, ordinary transmission payments, amounts otherwise

                                              Page 8 of 27
HB: 4899-5946-6429.5
 recovered through rates, energization status, phased development, and approved ramp schedules.
A flat percentage applied for a fixed number of years cannot be properly calibrated to the costs
imposed by a particular large load if it does not account for these project-specific protections and
circumstances.
    Crusoe understands that the recently filed TEBA report identifies a 75% contracted-demand
floor for 13 years as a potential means of balancing economic growth with customer protection. A
75% floor for 13 years is less severe than a 100% floor for 20 years, but it remains a flat demand-
based proxy. If the framework does not account for CIAC, security, interconnection payments,
phased energization, actual usage, ordinary rate recovery, and other protections already in place to
ensure large loads pay their share while adhering to cost causation principles, it cannot show that
the resulting payment is accurately calibrated to the net costs or risks caused by a particular
customer.
    The TEBA analysis confirms that the Proposal’s 100%/20-year demand ratchet is not the only,
or least restrictive, means of protecting other customers. But if adopted as a basis for minimum
billing demand for each large load, reliance on TEBA’s analysis could still convert a systemwide
average into a uniform rule that should not ignore project-by-project variances related to project-
specific costs, such as actual upgrades required, and payments or security provided, such as CIAC,
direct-assignment payments, charges paid through rates, and financial security.
    If the Commission nevertheless determines that a numerical floor is necessary, Crusoe supports
consideration of a lower, time-limited backstop, such as a 50%/five-year approach, as a more
calibrated alternative to the proposed 100%/20-year obligation. But even that approach should not
be treated as a substitute for proof on the record of a cost-causation analysis. In addition, it should
apply only to the then-energized, available, and usable phase of service; should phase in with the
customer’s approved ramp schedule; should be offset by CIAC, security, interconnection fees,
ordinary transmission payments, and other protections; and should phase out as actual 12CP
demand becomes the more appropriate measure of transmission cost responsibility.
    A ratcheted or weighted-average approach may be reasonable only if it is subordinate to that
net-risk framework. A ratchet should be capped, time-limited, ramp-adjusted, offset-adjusted, and
declining. A weighted average may be preferable if it transitions over time from reserved-capacity
measures toward actual 12CP demand, because it better recognizes both early-period reserved-
capacity risk and the long-term principle that actual coincident peak usage is the appropriate


                                            Page 9 of 27
HB: 4899-5946-6429.5
 measure of transmission cost responsibility. Prior-year NCP should not become an automatic long-
term floor where it reflects a commissioning event, testing peak, temporary operating condition,
partial-year ramp anomaly, or other nonrecurring demand that does not reflect continuing system
impact.


    4. Should separate rate treatment be applied to a large computational load, defined as

          an entity that is subject to §25.194 of this title (relating to Large Load Interconnection

          Standards) and in which 50% or greater of the demand at the site consists of power

          electronic based load, specifically computational load, such as data centers and

          cryptocurrency mining facilities?       Responses to this question should include

          applicable legal support or limitations regarding separate rate treatment for large

          computational loads.

    It is axiomatic that similarly situated loads should be treated similarly. Separate rate treatment

should not be applied based solely on whether a customer is a large computational load or because

50% or more of the site demand consists of power-electronic-based computational load. Rates and

minimum billing obligations should be based on cost causation, transmission impacts, reserved

capacity, actual usage, and demonstrated risk, rather than customer type, technology, or end use. If

computational loads impose different planning, operational, or reliability impacts, those impacts

should be addressed through generally applicable, cost-based criteria rather than a customer-

category surcharge.

    The Commission may appropriately address unique operational or interconnection

characteristics of large loads, including computational loads, through neutral interconnection,

modeling, telemetry, power-quality, or reliability standards that apply to similarly situated

customers. But separate rate treatment for data centers or cryptocurrency mining facilities should

only be implemented if supported by record evidence showing a material difference in cost

                                            Page 10 of 27
HB: 4899-5946-6429.5
 causation, transmission cost responsibility, service characteristics, or system impact, and only to

the extent that the differential treatment is warranted by and calibrated to those

differences. Differential treatment based solely on customer category, technology, or end use may

otherwise be unreasonably preferential, prejudicial, or discriminatory under PURA § 36.003 and

PUCT rate-design principles reflected in 16 TAC § 25.234.

    5. Should the definition for transmission interconnection costs be broadened to include

         transmission projects that are recommended at the conclusion of a batch study to

         serve the transmission capacity needs of a particular load?

    Crusoe supports the Commission’s proposed definition of transmission interconnection costs,

which appropriately focuses on facilities required to physically interconnect or upgrade the

interconnection of a transmission-level customer, or a distinct set of transmission-level customers,

to the existing transmission network. In applying that definition, the Commission should ensure

that a large load is responsible only for facilities, or portions of facilities, that are directly

attributable to and necessary to serve that load. Batch study projects may include or bundle

upgrades that support broader reliability, economic, or load-growth needs. A definition that

captures all batch study projects without separating load-specific costs from broader system

benefits could shift ordinary transmission expansion costs to individual customers in a manner

inconsistent with cost-causation principles.

    Crusoe recommends that the Commission distinguish direct interconnection facilities and load-

specific upgrades from broader transmission projects that provide regional or systemwide benefits.

Where a batch study project has mixed purposes or mixed beneficiaries, the large load should be

responsible only for the portion of the project that is directly attributable to and necessary to serve

that load, with the remaining costs recovered through ordinary transmission rates or otherwise



                                            Page 11 of 27
HB: 4899-5946-6429.5
 allocated to the customers that benefit, including the large load, where applicable. Any application

of the definition to batch study projects should include clear standards, documentation

requirements, offsets for CIAC, financial security, or other direct cost recovery, and safeguards to

prevent double recovery.

    Crusoe also supports Proposed § 25.252(b)(5), which recognizes that load-specific facilities

may later be used by the TSP to provide service to additional customers and that “the Commission

should establish an equitable mechanism to allocate or reimburse those costs.” If a large load funds

facilities that later serve others, the customer should receive an equitable allocation, credit, or

reimbursement. Likewise, if a transmission system upgrade project provides broader system

benefits from the outset, only the directly attributable load-specific portion should be assigned to

the large load.

    6. If a large load customer is able to reserve transmission capacity irrespective of
         whether the large load customer has energized or is fully using available capacity,
         how should these loads be reflected in the resource adequacy reports and assessments
         and transmission planning studies?

         A. Load Categories

    Crusoe recommends the use of objective, milestone-based criteria for determining load
categories, consistent with the criteria and categories established in connection with the Batch Zero
process: Reserved transmission capacity should be reflected in resource adequacy reports and
transmission planning studies in a way that distinguishes (i) energized/firm load; (ii)
committed/phased load: and (iii) speculative or contingent load, where:

         (i) Energized load is distinguished by energization and capacity to take service;
         (ii) Committed but not yet energized load may be phased or ramping load, and is qualified
              through:
                   o completion of required studies or inclusion in the applicable study process,




                                             Page 12 of 27
HB: 4899-5946-6429.5
                    o an executed interconnection agreement or comparable binding service or
                       interconnection commitment,
                   o posting of required financial security,
                   o payment of required CIAC or interconnection fees then due, and
                   o compliance with approved construction and ramp milestones.
           (iii) Contingent future load should include requested or reserved capacity that has not yet
              satisfied the objective milestones for committed load.

    For transmission planning, the key is to use realistic milestones, energization schedules,
security postings, interconnection status, and contractual commitments to determine whether
reserved capacity should be modeled as firm load, phased load, or contingent future load.

           B. Reporting

    Crusoe supports the Commission’s implied goals of improved transparency while avoiding
overstatement of near-term resource adequacy needs or transmission planning assumptions. To
that end, Crusoe recommends:

    i.        For load that is energized, the reported amount of load should be based on the level of
              service that is actually available and usable, including any approved operating limit or
              energized phase, rather than the customer’s full contracted demand, if future phases are
              not yet available.
    ii.       For committed load, ERCOT and TSPs should report and model load according to the
              approved phase or ramp schedule, and not as the full contracted demand.
    iii.      For contingent future load, while it may be appropriate for scenario or sensitivity
              analysis, it should not be treated as firm load in in base resource adequacy assessments
              or as fully available load in transmission planning assumptions.

    Implicit in the question of how load should be reflected in reports and studies is the appropriate
handling of project-specific information that is subject to competitive sensitivity concerns.
Project-level energization timelines and reservation status are commercially sensitive.
Competitors, brokers, and land speculators actively track this type of data. Crusoe recommends
that granular, project-level data be reported to ERCOT and the Commission under confidentiality
protections, with only aggregated or anonymized figures made available publicly.



                                             Page 13 of 27
HB: 4899-5946-6429.5
                                        IV.      CONCLUSION

    Crusoe appreciates the Commission’s efforts to ensure that large loads bear the costs and risks
they cause while protecting other customers from unrecovered transmission costs. Crusoe
respectfully urges the Commission to adopt a final rule that preserves that objective through
calibrated, cost-based measures rather than rigid or potentially duplicative requirements.

    In particular, any minimum payment should operate as a residual backstop for demonstrated,
unsecured risk, and should be offset by or otherwise account for CIAC, financial security,
interconnection fees, phased development, actual usage, and amounts otherwise recovered through
rates. To likewise avoid imposing duplicative costs on large loads, or charges for costs not
imposed by the customer, measures employed should not automatically impose full contracted-
demand billing before energization or for a fixed 20-year period. These calibrations would protect
ratepayers while maintaining fair, non-discriminatory, and predictable rules that support reliable
grid planning and continued investment in Texas.

               CRUSOE’S EXECUTIVE SUMMARY TO COMMENTS ON PROPOSED
                   AMENDMENTS TO §25.192 and §25.193 and NEW §25.252


•   Calibrate any minimum-payment obligation to residual cost or risk. Any minimum payment
    operate only as a residual backstop for demonstrated, unsecured transmission costs or stranded-
    capacity risk after accounting for CIAC, interconnection fees, financial security, ordinary
    transmission charges, energization status, phased development, and contractual commitments.

•   Separate “minimum payment” from “minimum billing demand.”

•   Limit any use of contracted demand to a cap or input. If contracted demand is used in
    calculating a minimum payment, adjust for energization status, phased ramp schedules, actual
    12CP/NCP usage, and posted financial protections, and not use as an automatic billing floor.

•   Use systemwide proxies only as a last resort. Crusoe recommends that any proxy based on
    systemwide averages be used only where project-specific cost or risk cannot be calculated, or is
    impracticable to calculate.

•   Do not impose automatic pre-energization deemed-demand billing.

•   Adopt a lower, time-limited alternative if the Commission requires a numerical demand
    floor. If the Commission determines that a demand-based minimum is necessary, Crusoe supports
    consideration of a more calibrated alternative, subject to phase-in, phase-out, offsets, actual usage,
    energization milestones, and project-specific cost-causation analysis.

•   Differentiate minimum charges only based on cost or risk, not size alone.

•   Use Batch Zero-style known-cost methods where appropriate.

•   Transition from reserved-capacity measures toward actual 12CP treatment.

•   Reject separate rate treatment based solely on computational-load status.

•   Limit transmission interconnection costs to directly attributable load-specific facilities.

•   Model and report large loads according to actual availability, usability, and approved ramps.

    B. Four Proposed Modifications to Calibrate a Minimum Payment Requirement.

              b. reduced in phases over a period of 20 years; or

         Crusoe recommends that the Commission modify the proposed minimum billing
requirement so that it operates as a calibrated, time-limited backstop rather than a fixed 20-year
obligation at the same level. Crusoe supports the Commission' s objective of protecting other
customers from unrecovered transmission costs or reserved-capacity risk, but the amount and
duration of any minimum billing requirement should be tied to the customer' s actual proj ect status,
approved ramp schedule, and declining residual risk. A rigid 20-year minimum billing obligation
based on full contracted peak demand, maximum NCP demand, or 12CP demand is likely broader
than necessary to protect other customers and may operate as a punitive or duplicative charge
rather than a calibrated cost-recovery mechanism.
         A better approach would allow minimum billing to phase in with the customer' s approved
energization and ramp schedule, and then phase out as the customer transitions to ordinary 12CP
treatment. For phased proj ects, the minimum billing amount should be based on the then-available
and usable phase of service, not the customer' s full ultimate contracted demand before that
capacity is energized or capable of being used.

to the proposed 100%/20-year obligation, provided the 50% level applies only to the relevant
energized, available, or usable phase and is offset by CIAC, interconnection fees, posted or
forfeited security, ordinary transmission payments, and other protections that reduce residual risk.
After the initial risk period, the customer should transition toward ordinary 12CP treatment,
because actual coincident peak usage becomes the more appropriate measure of transmission cost
responsibility as the project energizes, ramps, and becomes integrated into the ERCOT system.

         Crusoe recommends that the Commission not treat contracted peak demand or prior-year
NCP demand as an irrebuttable measure of large-load cost responsibility. Contracted demand and
NCP demand may be relevant inputs because they can indicate reserved capacity or site-level
demand, but demand is not the same thing as cost causation. Standing alone, these demand
measures do not establish the net unrecovered transmission costs or stranded-capacity risks caused
by a particular customer. The purpose of any minimum billing requirement should be to hold other
customers harmless from costs caused by the large load, not to assign to large loads costs they did
not cause.
    That distinction is important. To the extent residential customers are currently bearing a
disproportionate share of transmission costs, that is a problem that predates the arrival of large
loads in large numbers and should be addressed through generally applicable cost-allocation
reform. It is no more consistent with bedrock cost-causation principles to shift costs to large loads
that they did not cause than it is to misallocate transmission costs to residential customers. Cost
causation protects all customer classes; it is not satisfied by moving costs from one class to another
unless the shifted costs are shown to be caused by that class.
    For that reason, Crusoe's primary recommendation is not to replace the Proposal' s 100%/20-
year demand ratchet with a different flat demand ratchet. Crusoe recommends that the Commission
separate minimum billing from minimum billing demand and require any minimum payment to be
calibrated to demonstrated, residual, unsecured risk after accounting for CIAC, interconnection
fees, posted or forfeited financial security, ordinary transmission payments, amounts otherwise

 recovered through rates, energization status, phased development, and approved ramp schedules.
A flat percentage applied for a fixed number of years cannot be properly calibrated to the costs
imposed by a particular large load if it does not account for these proj ect-specific protections and
circumstances.
    Crusoe understands that the recently filed TEBA report identifies a 75% contracted-demand
floor for 13 years as a potential means of balancing economic growth with customer protection. A
75% floor for 13 years is less severe than a 100% floor for 20 years, but it remains a flat demand-
based proxy. If the framework does not account for CIAC, security, interconnection payments,
phased energization, actual usage, ordinary rate recovery, and other protections already in place to
ensure large loads pay their share while adhering to cost causation principles, it cannot show that
the resulting payment is accurately calibrated to the net costs or risks caused by a particular
customer.
    The TEBA analysis confirms that the Proposal's 100%/20-year demand ratchet is not the only,
or least restrictive, means of protecting other customers. But if adopted as a basis for minimum
billing demand for each large load, reliance on TEBA' s analysis could still convert a systemwide
average into a uniform rule that should not ignore project-by-project variances related to project-
specific costs, such as actual upgrades required, and payments or security provided, such as CIAC,
direct-assignment payments, charges paid through rates, and financial security.
    Ifthe Commission nevertheless determines that a numerical floor is necessary, Crusoe supports
consideration of a lower, time-limited backstop, such as a 50%/five-year approach, as a more
calibrated alternative to the proposed 100%/20-year obligation. But even that approach should not
be treated as a substitute for proof on the record of a cost-causation analysis. In addition, it should
apply only to the then-energized, available, and usable phase of service; should phase in with the
customer' s approved ramp schedule; should be offset by CIAC, security, interconnection fees,
ordinary transmission payments, and other protections; and should phase out as actual 12CP
demand becomes the more appropriate measure of transmission cost responsibility.
    A ratcheted or weighted-average approach may be reasonable only if it is subordinate to that
net-risk framework. A ratchet should be capped, time-limited, ramp-adjusted, offset-adjusted, and
declining. A weighted average may be preferable if it transitions over time from reserved-capacity
measures toward actual 12CP demand, because it better recognizes both early-period reserved-
capacity risk and the long-term principle that actual coincident peak usage is the appropriate

    4. Should separate rate treatment be applied to a large computational load, defined as

          an entity that is subject to §25.194 of this title (relating to Large Load Interconnection

          Standards) and in which 50% or greater of the demand at the site consists of power

          electronic based load, specifically computational load, such as data centers and

          cryptocurrency mining facilities?       Responses to this question should include

          applicable legal support or limitations regarding separate rate treatment for large

          computational loads.

    It is axiomatic that similarly situated loads should be treated similarly. Separate rate treatment

should not be applied based solely on whether a customer is a large computational load or because

50% or more of the site demand consists of power-electronic-based computational load. Rates and

minimum billing obligations should be based on cost causation, transmission impacts, reserved

capacity, actual usage, and demonstrated risk, rather than customer type, technology, or end use. If

computational loads impose different planning, operational, or reliability impacts, those impacts

should be addressed through generally applicable, cost-based criteria rather than a customer-

category surcharge.

    The Commission may appropriately address unique operational or interconnection

characteristics of large loads, including computational loads, through neutral interconnection,

modeling, telemetry, power-quality, or reliability standards that apply to similarly situated

customers. But separate rate treatment for data centers or cryptocurrency mining facilities should

only be implemented if supported by record evidence showing a material difference in cost

the extent that the differential treatment is warranted by and calibrated to those

differences. Differential treatment based solely on customer category, technology, or end use may

otherwise be unreasonably preferential, prejudicial, or discriminatory under PURA § 36.003 and

PUCT rate-design principles reflected in 16 TAC § 25.234.

    Crusoe supports the Commission's proposed definition of transmission interconnection costs,

which appropriately focuses on facilities required to physically interconnect or upgrade the

interconnection of a transmission-level customer, or a distinct set oftransmission-level customers,

to the existing transmission network. In applying that definition, the Commission should ensure

that a large load is responsible only for facilities, or portions of facilities, that are directly

attributable to and necessary to serve that load. Batch study projects may include or bundle

upgrades that support broader reliability, economic, or load-growth needs. A definition that

captures all batch study projects without separating load-specific costs from broader system

benefits could shift ordinary transmission expansion costs to individual customers in a manner

inconsistent with cost-causation principles.

    Crusoe recommends that the Commission distinguish direct interconnection facilities and load-

specific upgrades from broader transmission projects that provide regional or systemwide benefits.

Where a batch study proj ect has mixed purposes or mixed beneficiaries, the large load should be

responsible only for the portion of the project that is directly attributable to and necessary to serve

that load, with the remaining costs recovered through ordinary transmission rates or otherwise

should establish an equitable mechanism to allocate or reimburse those costs." If a large load funds

reimbursement. Likewise, if a transmission system upgrade project provides broader system

transmission planning studies in a way that distinguishes (i) energized/firm load; (ii)

    Crusoe supports the Commission' s implied goals of improved transparency while avoiding
overstatement of near-term resource adequacy needs or transmission planning assumptions. To
that end, Crusoe recommends:

              service that is actually available and usable, including any approved operating limit or
              energized phase, rather than the customer' s full contracted demand, i f future phases are

    ii.       For committed load, ERCOT and TSPs should report and model load according to the

    iii.      For contingent future load, while it may be appropriate for scenario or sensitivity

handling of proj ect-specific information that is subj ect to competitive sensitivity concerns.

    Crusoe appreciates the Commission' s efforts to ensure that large loads bear the costs and risks
they cause while protecting other customers from unrecovered transmission costs. Crusoe

calibrated, cost-based measures rather than rigid or potentially duplicative requirements.

unsecured risk, and should be offset by or otherwise account for CIAC, financial security,
interconnection fees, phased development, actual usage, and amounts otherwise recovered through

imposed by the customer, measures employed should not automatically impose full contracted-
